transcript.text: Sometimes when I open the dishwasher there's grey smelly water in the bottom even though it finished draining fine. Not every day though. Kitchen sink was replaced last month if that matters.

Yes, the sink replacement could be very relevant.

If the dishwasher drains normally at the end of a cycle but later has grey, smelly water sitting in the bottom, it is often dirty sink water flowing back into the dishwasher, rather than the dishwasher failing to drain.

Most likely causes, especially after sink work:

1. Dishwasher drain hose isn’t routed in a high loop / air gap
• The hose should rise as high as possible under the countertop before it connects to the sink drain or garbage disposal.
• Without that high loop (or a countertop air-gap fitting), water from the sink drain can siphon/backflow into the dishwasher.

2. Drain hose connection was changed or installed incorrectly
• It should connect to the disposal or sink-drain tailpiece in the correct position, typically before the trap arrangement but with a high loop in the hose.
• A plumber may have reconnected it low down, kinked it, or omitted the securing clip.

3. Partial blockage in the new sink drain, trap, disposal, or shared drain
• Water can drain “well enough” most of the time but back up when a large amount of sink water is released.
• This is especially likely if it happens after using the sink, running the disposal, or draining a full bowl/pan.

4. Garbage disposal issue, if you have one
• If the dishwasher hose was newly connected to a disposal, the installer must remove the dishwasher inlet’s knockout plug. That usually causes the dishwasher itself to fail to drain, though—not usually later backflow.
• A partially blocked disposal/drain can still cause backflow.

### Quick checks
• Notice whether the dishwasher water appears after you use the kitchen sink. If yes, that strongly points to backflow.
• Open the cabinet under the sink and look for the dishwasher’s corrugated drain hose. It should be clipped high up against the underside of the countertop, forming an upside-down “U” before descending to the drain connection.
• Check whether the sink drains slowly, gurgles, or backs up when you run water or the disposal.

### What to do now
• Remove the standing water and clean the dishwasher filter/sump area if accessible.
• Run a hot rinse cycle afterward, ideally with dishwasher cleaner or a cup of white vinegar placed in a dishwasher-safe bowl on the upper rack (don’t mix vinegar with bleach products).
• Contact the person/company that replaced the sink and describe it as:
  “The dishwasher drains after a cycle, but dirty sink water intermittently backs up into it. Please check the dishwasher drain connection, high loop/air gap, and the sink drain/trap for partial blockage.”

Avoid running the dishwasher until it is corrected if it is regularly refilling with foul water—anything washed afterward can be exposed to dirty drain water.

I checked under the sink. The dishwasher hose just lies on the cupboard floor and goes straight into the waste spigot, with no high loop. It does seem to happen after I drain a sink full of washing-up water, and the sink drains a little slow. It's a Hotpoint HFC 3C26 W, 3 years old. Should I loop the hose up?

Yes — based on what you found, a properly secured high loop is very likely needed. The hose lying on the cabinet floor gives sink water an easy path to run or siphon back into the dishwasher, especially when you empty a full sink.

For your Hotpoint, the drain hose should rise up and be fixed as high as practical under the worktop/countertop, then drop down to the waste spigot. This creates a high loop that helps prevent backflow.

A few important points:

• Secure it properly with a suitable hose clip/bracket fixed to the cabinet side or underside of the worktop. Don’t puncture, crush, or tightly kink the hose.
• The hose should form a smooth upside-down “U”: dishwasher → up high under the worktop → down to the sink waste connection.
• Keep the final connection secure on the spigot with its hose clamp.
• Don’t make an extreme loop or extend the hose with improvised fittings. If the existing hose cannot reach the high point without strain or kinking, have an installer fit an approved longer hose/extension.
• An air-gap fitting is another solution where required by local plumbing rules, but a high loop is commonly used.

However, the slow-draining sink also needs attention. A high loop will reduce or stop dirty water reaching the dishwasher, but it does not cure a partial blockage in the sink trap, waste pipe, or shared drain. Since the sink was replaced recently, ask the installer/plumber to check:

1. the trap and new waste fittings for a partial obstruction or poor fall,
2. the dishwasher spigot connection,
3. that the dishwasher hose is clipped in a high loop,
4. whether the downstream kitchen drain needs clearing.

Until it is fixed, avoid draining a full sink rapidly if possible. Once the plumbing is corrected, run a hot dishwasher cycle and clean the dishwasher filter/sump area to remove the smelly residual water.
